title: Blurring from the Inside

patient.name: Mr Ramesh s/o Krishnaswamy
patient.presenting_complaint: Referred from polyclinic for blurring vision in right eye on routine diabetic eye screening

history.hpc: Mr Ramesh was flagged at his polyclinic diabetic eye screening 2 weeks ago. He admits his right eye has been slightly blurry for the past 2 months, which he attributed to tiredness. He denies floaters, flashing lights, or curtain-like visual loss. He has had Type 2 diabetes for 14 years. He admits his blood sugars have been 'a bit high lately' and he has not been strict with his diet.
history.pmhx: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 10.2% at last check 3 months ago), hypertension, hyperlipidaemia
history.family_hx: Mother had diabetes and was 'blind in one eye'
history.social_hx: Taxi driver — driving licence at risk, smokes 10 cigarettes/day for 30 years, occasional alcohol

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Clear cornea, normal anterior chambers, no rubeosis iridis

fundus.right: New vessels on disc (NVD) approximately 1/4 disc area, pre-retinal haemorrhage superior to disc, scattered dot and blot haemorrhages throughout all quadrants, hard exudates approaching fovea, macular oedema on clinical assessment
fundus.left: Dot and blot haemorrhages in all quadrants, hard exudates, no new vessels — severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy

investigations.fundus_fluorescein_angiography: Right: large area of NVD with leakage, areas of capillary non-perfusion in mid-periphery, macular leakage consistent with diabetic macular oedema
investigations.oct_macula: Right: central macular thickness 412 microns with intraretinal and subretinal fluid (centre-involving DMO). Left: 298 microns with early thickening.

diagnosis: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) with centre-involving diabetic macular oedema (CI-DMO), right eye. Severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), left eye.

immediate: Urgent intravitreal anti-VEGF injection (ranibizumab or aflibercept) to right eye for CI-DMO
Plan panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) to right eye after anti-VEGF for NVD
Urgent referral to left eye for preventive PRP given severe NPDR
Urgent systemic referral: optimise glycaemic control (target HbA1c <7%), control BP (<130/80 mmHg)
Advise patient not to drive until vision improves and is assessed — inform DVLA equivalent
follow_up: Right eye anti-VEGF: monthly injections until DMO resolves (treat-and-extend thereafter)
Review NVD regression after anti-VEGF + PRP at 6–8 weeks
Left eye: PRP within 2 weeks, monitor for progression to PDR
Shared care with GP/endocrinologist for metabolic control
Annual diabetic eye screening both eyes ongoing
patient_education: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of blindness — can be prevented with control of sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol
Eye injections treat the swelling and new vessels but do not cure diabetes
Smoking accelerates diabetic complications — smoking cessation support offered
Regular eye checks are mandatory — do not skip even if vision feels normal

key_points: Asks duration and nature of diabetes, HbA1c control
Asks about floaters or flashes (vitreous haemorrhage risk)
Occupation history — driving implications for vision
Requests fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) to delineate NVD and ischaemia
Requests OCT macula for DMO quantification
Examines fellow eye for bilateral disease
Identifies proliferative diabetic retinopathy (not just NPDR)
Notes severity difference between right and left eye
Driving advice and occupational implications addressed
